questions.q: The following are essential to consider the diagnosis of heart failure in a 3-year-old girl except:
o: Chest X-ray with cardiothoracic ratio of 1.8:2
questions.e: The question's answer key identifies C as the exception. The finding is not specific on its own for heart failure.

questions.q:
Q40 (file no. 37)
Breast feeding is contraindicated in:
questions.e: Classic galactosaemia in the infant is a contraindication to breastfeeding because lactose/galactose exposure is harmful. Infants with phenylketonuria can often receive measured breast milk as part of an individualized feeding plan with phenylalanine-free medical formula and metabolic monitoring. A breast lump, early pregnancy, cracked nipples, and maternal warfarin use are not automatic contraindications to breastfeeding; assess and manage each situation individually.

questions.q:
Q41 (file no. 38)
Which of the following is the best source of vitamin D:
questions.e: Vitamin D content depends on fortification and the product label. Among these options, vitamin-D-fortified milk is the intended source; unfortified margarine, tomatoes, cabbage, and ordinary cheese are not equivalent sources. Dietary vitamin D is also supplied by oily fish and egg yolk, while many infants require age-appropriate vitamin D supplementation according to local guidance.

questions.q:
Q7 (file no. 7)
Concerning Pertusis, which of the following statements is incorrect:
o: It is caused by Bordetella Pertussis.
Paroxysmal cough followed by whoop is characteristic feature in older children.
Blood culture is the investigation of choice.
Macrolides are the antibiotics of choice.
In infants, apnea is a common clinical feature.
questions.e: Pertussis is caused by Bordetella pertussis. Blood cultures are not the diagnostic investigation for this respiratory infection. The appropriate specimen is a posterior nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate for culture and/or PCR; culture is the reference gold-standard method, while PCR is faster and highly sensitive. Thus option C is the incorrect statement.

questions.q:
Q8 (file no. 8)
In whooping cough one of the following statement is CORRECT:
o: Severe disease, hospitalisation and complications are most common in young infants.
Diagnosis by taking a throat swab.
questions.e: Young infants, especially those who are not fully protected by vaccination, have the greatest risk of severe pertussis complications and hospitalisation. This distinguishes severity from overall infection frequency, which the original option did not specify. Pertussis spreads mainly through respiratory droplets; the typical incubation period is usually about 7–10 days (with a wider range), and diagnosis uses a nasopharyngeal specimen rather than a throat swab.

questions.q:
Q15 (file no. 9 (repeated, chickenpox))
Chicken pox infection:
o: Has an incubation period of one week.
Remains infectious until all lesions have crusted; in vaccinated cases with non-crusting lesions, until no new lesions appear for 24 hours.
questions.e: Varicella is usually infectious from 1–2 days before rash onset until all lesions have crusted. In vaccinated people who develop non-vesicular lesions that do not crust, the infectious period ends when no new lesions have appeared for 24 hours. The incubation period is 10–21 days, and the rash is typically maculopapulovesicular and appears in different stages.

questions.q: Which of the following vaccines is NOT a live vaccine?
questions.e: Hib vaccine is a non-live conjugate vaccine. OPV, BCG and measles-containing vaccines are live attenuated vaccines; varicella vaccine is also live attenuated. The stem specifies OPV (not inactivated IPV) so the polio option is unambiguous. Therefore Hib is the single non-live answer.

questions.q:
Q73 (file no. 63)
Regarding childhood immunization, one is CORRECT
o: Hib vaccine is a conjugate vaccine that can be administered before 2 years as it can stimulate T-cell dependent immunity
Rotavirus vaccine is an inactivated injectable vaccine.
PCV given at 2, 4 and 12 months is a polysaccharide capsular vaccine
HPV vaccine to adolescent girls to preventing congenital anomalies in fetus
IPV is effective in controlling epidemics
questions.e: Hib vaccine is a protein-conjugated polysaccharide vaccine. Conjugation makes the immune response T-cell dependent, allowing an effective response in infants younger than 2 years. Rotavirus vaccines are live oral vaccines, PCV is a conjugate vaccine, HPV vaccination is for prevention of HPV-related disease, and IPV is inactivated; it does not provide the same interruption of intestinal transmission as OPV.

questions.q: Q1. Regarding neonatal resuscitation which of the following is incorrect:
o: Give intravascular epinephrine if the heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation and 60 seconds of coordinated chest compressions.
Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely recommended during initial neonatal resuscitation.
Face mask & bag is method of choice in diaphragmatic hernia.
Naloxone is not part of initial neonatal resuscitation and must never delay effective ventilation.
Consider volume expansion when blood loss is known or suspected and the newborn does not respond to initial resuscitation, including epinephrine.
questions.e: In suspected congenital diaphragmatic hernia, avoid bag-mask ventilation because it can insufflate the stomach and bowel, worsening intrathoracic compression; establish the airway with endotracheal intubation and decompress the stomach. Current neonatal resuscitation prioritizes effective ventilation; chest compressions are used when the heart rate remains below 60/min despite adequate ventilation, and epinephrine is considered if the rate remains below 60/min after coordinated compressions. Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely recommended during initial resuscitation. Naloxone is not an initial-resuscitation intervention and must not delay ventilation. Volume expansion is considered when blood loss is suspected and the infant remains unresponsive to resuscitation.

questions.q: Q3. Possible causes of neonatal seizures except:
questions.e: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is the commonest cause; hypomagnesemia (with hypocalcemia) and intraventricular/intracranial hemorrhage are well-established causes. Vitamin E deficiency does not cause neonatal seizures (the vitamin deficiency that does is pyridoxine/vitamin B6 dependency).

questions.q: Q10. Care of preterm includes the following except:
o: A trained person dedicated to newborn care and able to provide ventilation should be present at every birth; additional team members are mobilized according to risk.
To give Vit K at birth.
To be nursed at neutral thermal environment.
questions.e: Oxygen is given only when indicated (hypoxemia/respiratory distress) and titrated to target saturations - routine oxygen for all small babies is harmful (retinopathy of prematurity, oxidative lung injury). (a), (c), (d), (e) are all standard preterm care.

questions.q: Q16. The following is not a manifestation of diaphragmatic hernia:
o: Failure to response to neonatal resuscitation.
questions.e: CDH causes lung HYPOPLASIA (not hyperplasia) on the side of the herniated bowel plus pulmonary hypertension. Respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen (bowel in chest), polyhydramnios and poor response to routine resuscitation are all typical.

questions.q:
Q19. For a full term exclusively breast-fed thriving baby, the following feeding practice is
recommended:
o: Iron supplementation from the age of 2 months.
Fluoride supplementation of the mother from delivery.
Vitamin C supplementation from the age of 2 months.
Introduce complementary foods at about 6 months while continuing breastfeeding.
Weaning to cow's milk at 4 month.
questions.e: For most healthy infants, complementary foods are introduced at about 6 months while breastfeeding continues. Iron supplementation for exclusively breastfed term infants depends on the applicable national guideline and infant risk; routine advice should not be shifted to 2 months without a specific indication. Cow’s milk should not replace breast milk or infant formula as the main drink before 12 months.

questions.q:
Q28. 1-day old newborn to diabetic mother was delivered vaginally at full term with shoulder
dystocia, birth weight 4.7 Kg. At 5 minutes after birth: pulse was 110/min, cyanotic hands and feet,
good muscle tone with strong cry and grimace. After one hour baby noticed to be plethoric, plumb,
unable to move right upper limb, with internal rotation to forearm, pronation of hand, flexion of
wrist, permanent extension of fingers. Respiratory rate 70/min, HR 180, nothing remarkable on
upper limb x-ray with see-saw appearance on chest x-ray. All of the following are expected findings
except:
questions.e: Shoulder dystocia in a macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother causes brachial plexus injury (Erb C5-6 and/or Klumpke C8-T1) and phrenic nerve injury (C3-5) -> diaphragmatic paralysis with see-saw breathing and respiratory distress. Vagal nerve injury is not part of this picture (it would present with hoarseness/stridor, feeding problems).

questions.q: Q46. One of the following features is not typically seen in a preterm baby:
questions.e: Meconium aspiration occurs in post-term/term babies with fetal distress; preterm babies rarely pass meconium in utero. Hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia and sepsis are common in prematurity.

questions.q: Q48. Which of the following is not routinely included in standard newborn screening panels in many programmes?
questions.e: Wilson disease is not included in routine newborn screening panels in most programmes; it usually presents later in childhood or adolescence. Hearing loss, congenital hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria, and cystic fibrosis are screened for in many established programmes, but the exact panel varies by country and may change over time.

questions.q: Q53. What is the immediate action you will take:
questions.e: Give vitamin K (1 mg IM/IV slowly) immediately; add fresh frozen plasma/PCC only if bleeding is severe. Antibiotics are not indicated, transfusion only if hemodynamically significant blood loss, immunoglobulin has no role.

questions.q: Q55. A neonate at birth has a weak cry, heart rate of 120/min, pink colour centrally with blue extremities, limp muscle tone with no flexion, and absent reflex response. What is the Apgar score?
questions.e: Apgar: heart rate above 100/min = 2; acrocyanosis = 1; limp muscle tone = 0; absent reflex response = 0; weak/irregular respiratory effort = 1. Total = 4.

questions.q: Q63. Criteria for neonatal metabolic screening, the condition:
o: Is an important health problem, judged by its frequency and/or severity.
questions.e: Screening is considered when a condition is an important health problem, an effective intervention is available, early detection improves outcomes, and a suitable validated test and follow-up pathway exist. Importance is judged by frequency and/or severity; a high incidence threshold is not an absolute requirement. With the revised option B, “All the above” is the best answer.

questions.q: Q96. Which of the following is NOT a component of the Apgar score?
questions.e: The five Apgar components are Appearance (colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration (respiratory effort). Haemoglobin concentration is not part of the Apgar score.

questions.q: Q102. The neonatal apnea defined as:
o: Cessation of breathing for 20 seconds or longer, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia, oxygen desaturation, cyanosis, or pallor.
Cyanosis with cessation of breathing for more than 30 seconds.
Bradycardia associated with cessation of breathing for more than 40 seconds.
Cessation of breathing for 5 seconds with loss of muscle tone.
Cessation of breathing for 10 seconds associated with chocking.
questions.e: Neonatal apnoea is generally defined as cessation of breathing for about 20 seconds or longer, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia, oxygen desaturation, cyanosis, or pallor. The duration alone does not determine clinical significance.

questions.q: Q118. Which of the following is a separate population-based newborn screening test rather than a routine bedside examination or immediate prophylactic intervention?
o: Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine if the mother is hepatitis B positive.
questions.e: Weighing, newborn examination including hip assessment, intramuscular vitamin K, and hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG for an infant born to an HBsAg-positive mother are routine bedside or immediate postnatal measures. Screening for congenital hypothyroidism is a separate newborn-screening test performed after birth according to the local screening programme; the sampling day and programme coverage vary by jurisdiction.

questions.q: Q126. In neonatal clinical practice the following statements are true except:
o: breast milk jaundice is a diagnosis of exclusion.
If swaddling is used, place the infant supine, allow free hip flexion and abduction, avoid overheating, and stop swaddling when the infant shows signs of rolling.
Erythema neonatorum is a benign skin rash.
Biochemical screening for phenyl ketonuria is carried at age of 48-72hrs.
questions.e: Not all hypoglycaemic newborns are symptomatic; some have no obvious clinical signs, which is why risk-based glucose screening is important. Breast-milk jaundice is a diagnosis of exclusion, erythema toxicum neonatorum is benign, and newborn screening for phenylketonuria is performed after feeding has been established according to the local programme. Swaddling is not categorically prohibited when safe-sleep precautions are followed.

questions.q: Q128. Among term newborns, which is the most common cause of neonatal convulsions?
questions.e: See Q72.

questions.q: Q130. In congenital infections all of the following are true except:
o: Maternal varicella rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery requires prompt neonatal assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis when indicated.
Babies of addicted mothers are at increased risk of hepatitis B, C & HIV infections.
Congenital rubella and cytomegalovirus infection can be diagnosed by urine viral culture.
Hepatosplenomegaly with jaundice may be the presenting features of congenital infection.
IgM antibodies can cross the placenta and give passive immunity to the babies.
questions.e: Only IgG crosses the placenta; IgM is a large pentamer that does not, which is why a raised IgM in the newborn indicates intrauterine infection. (a) maternal varicella around delivery (5 days before to 2 days after) requires VZIG for the baby; (b), (c), (d) are true.

questions.q: Q141. Regarding congenital infection, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
o: Rubella: the highest risk of fetal damage if maternal infection occurs before 8 week gestation.
Cytomegalovirus: 90% are symptomatic at birth and develop abnormally.
Toxoplasmosis: blood serology shows high specific IgM and persistently raised Toxoplasma IgG.
Varicella-zoster immune globulin is indicated for eligible newborns whose mother develops a varicella rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery.
Parvovirus B19, one of the causes of fetal hydrops.
questions.e: About 90% of congenital CMV infections are ASYMPTOMATIC at birth (only ~10% symptomatic), so (b) is incorrect. (a) rubella carries ~90% risk of defects in the first 8-10 weeks; (c) is the typical serology; (d) VZIG is indicated for maternal chickenpox from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery (the exam's "5 days after" is approximate); (e) parvovirus B19 causes fetal hydrops.

questions.q: Q152. In very low birth weight babies which of the following complications is not true?
o: Iron deficiency anemia before the age of 3 months.
questions.e: The listed early complications include hypothermia, hypocalcaemia, hypoglycaemia, and necrotizing enterocolitis. Very-low-birth-weight infants have low iron stores and high iron requirements, so iron supplementation is generally started early once enteral feeds are established according to neonatal guidance. Iron deficiency and anaemia of prematurity are distinct processes; the statement about iron-deficiency anaemia before 3 months is not an absolute biological rule, but D remains the intended exception in this item’s conventional teaching context.

questions.q:
Q154. A full term normal vaginal delivery baby on exclusive breast feeding, he presented at 4
weeks of age with jaundice. He was well, not pale, no hepatosplenomegaly. His investigation
profile shows: Hb 14.5gm/dl, total serum bilirubin 8.3mg/dl, direct 0.4mg/dl, liver enzyme AST 12
unit, ALT 15unit. What is the abnormal laboratory result?
questions.e: The indirect bilirubin is 8.3 − 0.4 = 7.9 mg/dL. This is persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at 4 weeks and warrants assessment, including measurement of total and direct bilirubin. In a thriving breastfed infant, breast-milk jaundice is a possible benign explanation, but prolonged jaundice must not be assumed benign until cholestasis and other causes are excluded. Hb and the listed liver enzymes are not elevated in this vignette.

questions.q: Q155. A 4-week-old term infant who is exclusively breastfed is thriving but remains jaundiced. Total serum bilirubin is 8.3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin is 0.4 mg/dL; haemoglobin and liver enzymes are within the stated reference range, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Biliary atresia gives conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (high direct fraction), pale stools and abnormal LFTs - not found here. Breast-milk jaundice, UTI, hypothyroidism and Crigler-Najjar all cause prolonged UNCONJUGATED jaundice.

questions.q:
Q95. Data 5: Hadel, 2 years old, presented with a history of abdominal pain and fever for the last 4
days, her urine was yellow, turbid, and foul smell. Her urine analysis showed: Protein (nil), Nitrites
(+), Blood (+), Pus cell >100 cells/HPF, RBC = 3-5 cells/HPF. No cast was seen. CBC showed: WBC
= 18x10^3/uL, Plat = 200x10^3/uL, Hb = 12.5 gm/dl, ESR = 50 mm/hour, CRP = 70 mg/L, Blood Urea
= 25 mg/dl, Creatinine = 0.8 mg/dl. Her investigations showed?
questions.e: Pyuria (>100 pus cells/HPF), leukocytosis (18,000/µL), and raised ESR/CRP support acute urinary infection. A serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL is above the usual reference range for a 2-year-old child and should not be labelled normal. Therefore all four findings are present and option E is correct.

questions.q:
66. All the following results are abnormal except:
Scenario: 7 years old girl had been well until 2 years ago where she has intermittent episode of non-bloody
diarrhea and abdominal distension. She feels nauseous and vomiting especially during her mean meal. She
has muscle wasting (particulary at the buttock) her weight was 15 kg and height 105 cm. Investigations Hb
8.2 g/dl, PCV 25, MCH 195, MCV 64, serum iron 6 umole, TIBC 84, with low serum folate and normal serum
B12.
questions.e: The vignette explicitly reports normal serum vitamin B12, so this is the normal result. Hb 8.2 g/dL and MCV 64 fL are low, weight and height are low for age, serum iron 6 µmol/L is low, and TIBC 84 is high, supporting iron deficiency in the context of malabsorption.

questions.q: Which of the following is a principal cause of megaloblastic anaemia?
o: Caused by folic acid or B12 deficiency.
questions.e: Megaloblastic anaemia is caused by folate or vitamin B12 deficiency (impaired DNA synthesis). It is macrocytic and is associated with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia in severe cases).

questions.q:
45. The management includes:
Scenario: Case IV: 2 years old boy presented with bone pain at his left shoulder & back for 2 days duration.
He had history of admission because of abdominal pain and received twice blood transfusion. His older sister
has the same disease. On examination he was pale, mild jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, just palpable liver
and spleen was not palpable.
o: Individualised oral or IV hydration according to clinical status, correcting dehydration without routine overhydration.
Starting IV fluid as twice maintenance.
questions.e: A vaso-occlusive crisis requires prompt analgesia, assessment and correction of dehydration, and monitoring for complications such as acute chest syndrome. Fluid intake should be individualised to hydration status, respiratory status and other fluid inputs; systematic overhydration is not recommended because it has no proven benefit and may cause harm. Routine transfusion is not indicated solely because haemoglobin is below 10 g/dL, and splenectomy is not routine crisis treatment.

questions.q: 57. Which statement is not true regarding acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)?
o: It accounts 80% of leukemia in children.
It's peak at age of 2-5 years.
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) accounts for most acute leukaemia cases in children with Down syndrome.
Bone marrow examination is essential to confirm the diagnosis.
Additional treatment with intrathecal chemotherapy is used to prevent CNS relapse.
questions.e: The revised option C is the false statement. Children with Down syndrome have an increased risk of both ALL and AML, but approximately one-half to two-thirds of acute leukaemia cases in this population are ALL, making ALL the most common type. AML risk is markedly increased relative to children without Down syndrome, but AML does not account for most cases.

questions.q:
In a child with suspected hereditary spherocytosis, which initial investigation is most useful for assessing red-cell morphology?
Scenario: Ayoub, 5 years old, presented with pallor and jaundice. On examination he was well, jaundiced, with splenomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, no hepatomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Hb 8 g/dL, WBC 11,000/µL, platelets 300 × 10^3/µL, MCV 87 fL and reticulocytes 15%.
questions.e: A peripheral blood film is the initial test that assesses red-cell morphology and may show spherocytes. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is also important to distinguish hereditary spherocytosis from autoimmune haemolysis, but it answers a different diagnostic question. If the film and clinical picture support hereditary spherocytosis, confirmatory testing may include eosin-5-maleimide binding or other validated membrane tests.

questions.q: 96. Regarding reticulocyte the following are correct EXCEPT
o: It is larger than mature red blood corpuscle (RBC).
Increased reticulocytes (Reticulocytosis) seen in untreated iron deficiency anemia.
Increased reticulocytes (Reticulocytosis) seen in hereditary spherocytosis.
Reticulocytes generally have higher G6PD activity than mature erythrocytes.
questions.e: Reticulocytes are slightly larger than mature red cells and contain residual ribosomal RNA. Reticulocytes and young erythrocytes have higher G6PD activity than older mature erythrocytes, so option E is true. Reticulocytosis is expected in haemolysis, including hereditary spherocytosis, but untreated iron-deficiency anaemia generally produces an inadequate rather than increased reticulocyte response; option C is the exception.

questions.q: Q9. What is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.e: A chest X-ray is an appropriate initial imaging investigation when inhaled foreign body is suspected, but a normal radiograph does not exclude aspiration. If clinical suspicion remains high, specialist assessment and bronchoscopy are required; bronchoscopy is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. CT should not delay bronchoscopy when suspicion is high.

questions.q: 14) Drugs known to cause hearing loss include all Except?
questions.e: Penicillin is not a classic ototoxic drug. Aminoglycosides, loop diuretics and platinum-based chemotherapy such as cisplatin are recognised causes of ototoxicity; chloroquine has also been associated with auditory toxicity. Therefore penicillin remains the exception.

questions.q: 23) The following are true regarding Major immunoglobulin abnormalities except:
o: Antibody (B-cell) deficiencies form the largest broad category of primary immunodeficiencies.
It is mainly due to failure in T-cell development and its function.
Presents in the first 2 years of life.
In the hyper IgM syndrome, Children present with pneumocystis Carinii infection.
questions.e: Most primary immunodeficiencies are antibody/B-cell disorders as a broad category. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia is one important antibody deficiency, but it is not the most common individual primary immunodeficiency. Immunoglobulin abnormalities are not mainly caused by T-cell developmental failure; therefore option B remains the exception.

questions.t: Adrenal Disorders (CAH, Addison Disease & Cushing Syndrome)
questions.q: Q10. His arterial blood gases (ABG) status shows?
o: Metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis.
questions.e: The pH and low bicarbonate indicate primary metabolic acidosis. The measured PaCO2 is lower than the expected compensatory value by Winter’s formula (expected PaCO2 ≈ 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2 mmHg), indicating an additional respiratory alkalosis. Thus the best description is metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

questions.t: Adrenal Disorders (CAH, Addison Disease & Cushing Syndrome)
questions.q: Q73. What specific investigation you would order at this stage:
questions.e: The clinical features suggest Cushing syndrome. Confirm hypercortisolism biochemically before imaging. Appropriate initial screening includes at least two 24-hour urinary free cortisol measurements, two late-night salivary cortisol measurements, or a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, selected according to the clinical setting. A random serum cortisol level is not an adequate screening test.

questions.q: Q74. The following is laboratory finding seen in hyperglycemia during diabetic ketoacidosis:
questions.e: Hyperglycaemia raises extracellular tonicity and shifts water from the intracellular to extracellular space, lowering the measured serum sodium concentration. This is translocational (hypertonic) hyponatraemia, not pseudohyponatraemia. Pseudohyponatraemia is a measurement artefact associated with markedly elevated lipids or proteins when indirect ion-selective electrode methods are used.

questions.q: Q75. Delayed puberty is often defined as:
o: Absence of pubertal development by the age of 10 years in female and 12 years in males.
Absence of pubertal development by the age of 13 years in female and 11 years in males.
Absence of pubertal development by the age of 15 years in female and 13 years in males.
No breast development by 13 years in girls, or no testicular enlargement to at least 4 mL by 14 years in boys.
Absence of pubertal development by the age of 12 years in female and 13 years in males.
questions.e: Delayed puberty is commonly defined as absence of breast development by age 13 years in girls, or absence of testicular enlargement to at least 4 mL by age 14 years in boys. These are the standard clinical thresholds used to trigger evaluation.

questions.q: Q80. All these are insulin types used as a basal insulin EXCEPT:
questions.e: Aspart is a rapid-acting mealtime/bolus insulin, not a basal insulin. Glargine, detemir, degludec, and NPH are used as basal insulin preparations; degludec replaces the obsolete ultralente formulation in this contemporary option set.

questions.q:
Q86. Case: A 10 years old child present to casualty with a one-day history of vomiting. Vital signs
showed Temp 37 C, HR 110, BP 95/60 mmHg. He is lethargic but oriented. Physical examination
reveals the odor of acetone on the breath, dry lips and mucous membrane, but other examinations
are unremarkable. Laboratory: Blood glucose 560 mg/dl, pH 7.05, PaCO2 20 mmHg, PaO2 95
mmHg, BE -20, Na 128 mmol/l, K 4.9 mmol/l, HCO3 8, urine shows ketones ++++ and glucose ++++.
The following are appropriate interpretation of laboratory results EXCEPT
questions.e: The primary disorder is metabolic acidosis: pH 7.05 with HCO3 8 mmol/L. PaCO2 20 mmHg is reduced as respiratory compensation, so this is not respiratory acidosis; option E is the exception. The measured sodium is low in the setting of hyperglycaemia because of a translocational water shift, not pseudohyponatraemia. Using the common 1.6 mmol/L correction per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100, corrected sodium is approximately 135 mmol/L. Potassium 4.9 mmol/L is within the usual measured range, although total-body potassium is depleted in DKA.
